Dutch Chemical Workers End Four-Day Walkout; Production Back on Track

A four-day walkout by workers in the Dutch chemicals industry has ended after unions and employers reached a settlement on wages and working conditions, industry sources confirmed on Tuesday. The strike, which began last Thursday, affected several major production sites in the Rotterdam and Delfzijl regions, including facilities operated by Akzo Nobel NV and Chemica Noord.

The industrial action was sparked by a deadlock in negotiations over pay increases and overtime rules. According to union representatives, over 1,200 employees participated in the walkout, leading to temporary shutdowns and reduced output at multiple chemical plants. The Netherlands Chemical Workers Union said the strike was necessary to “secure fair compensation and safer workplace conditions for our members.”

Akzo Nobel NV reported on Monday that its Delfzijl site had resumed full operations following the agreement. “We are pleased to have reached a constructive understanding with our employees, enabling us to restart production safely and efficiently,” said facility manager Janine Bakker in a statement.

Industry analysts estimate the strike reduced national chemical production capacity by as much as 30% during the stoppage. The Dutch Association of Chemical Producers welcomed the swift resolution. “This agreement allows the sector to return to normal and meet both domestic and international supply commitments,” spokesperson Robert Visser said.

Under the new deal, workers will receive a 5% pay increase over two years and enhanced overtime provisions. Union leaders called the outcome “a positive step forward” for chemical industry employees across the Netherlands.
